en.title: Software Engineering: the whole course
en.short: What software engineering covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What software engineering is
sections.text:
Software engineering is the disciplined application of engineering ideas to software: understanding what a system must do, designing it, building it, testing it, and maintaining it over time. It is not only programming. Programming is the main craft, but large systems also need requirements, architecture, planning, quality control, security and teamwork.

Software is intangible and easy to change, which makes control difficult. A small change can break a distant part of a system. Software engineering therefore studies processes, models, measurements and professional responsibility. It draws on computer science, mathematics, management and human factors. The aim is software that is correct, usable, maintainable and delivered at a sensible cost.

sections.heading: How a degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc in software engineering commonly runs for four years; BEng routes in engineering faculties can take five. Confirm this in your department’s handbook. The National Universities Commission (NUC) sets minimum academic standards for university programmes; the Core Curriculum and Minimum Academic Standards (CCMAS) is the current framework, with a separate volume for computing programmes such as software engineering. Polytechnics award the ND and HND under National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) standards and usually give more weight to practical work. Many Nigerian programmes include industrial training through the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme (SIWES); check your own regulations.

In England, a BSc usually takes three years, often with a placement option. Scottish degrees often take four years. In Ghana and Kenya, four-year degrees are common. In South Africa, a three-year BSc may be followed by an Honours year. A master’s degree usually adds one or two years of advanced courses and a dissertation. Accreditation and registration rules differ, so check your national body.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds foundations. You start with what software engineering is, then programming fundamentals, discrete mathematics, data structures and algorithms, object-oriented programming and modelling, databases and SQL, computer systems and networks, web and mobile foundations, and software tools and version control. These topics support each other.

The core stage covers the life cycle. You study software process models, agile and lean practices, requirements engineering, system modelling and UML, software architecture, design principles and patterns, construction and code quality, testing fundamentals, automated testing and continuous integration, verification and validation, maintenance and evolution, configuration and release management, project management and estimation, quality and process improvement, security and dependability, human-centred design and usability, and professional practice and ethics. A capstone project usually brings these together in a team or individual project.

At master’s level, common topics include advanced software architecture, formal specification and verification, and empirical software engineering research. The exact order varies between universities.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Write code every week and finish small projects. A command-line tool, a simple web application or a mobile form with a database teaches more than reading alone. Put every project under version control from the first day. Write tests for the parts you can check automatically, and run them after each change.

For process and requirements topics, compare models on real examples. Ask what changes when a client changes a requirement late. Draw UML diagrams by hand and check that every relationship has a meaning. For architecture and design, study small systems and identify their modules, interfaces and trade-offs. For testing, practise choosing inputs that expose boundary cases. For formal methods, write each proof step in full. For empirical research, learn to read a study’s method before trusting its result. Start the capstone early, keep a log, and follow your university’s rules on AI tools.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often make these mistakes:
Treating software engineering as only programming and ignoring requirements, testing and maintenance.
Memorising a process model instead of understanding when it fits.
Writing code before deciding what the system must do.
Drawing UML diagrams that look neat but do not match the code or the requirements.
Testing only the happy path and forgetting empty inputs, large values and error cases.
Confusing verification with validation. Verification asks whether the product meets its specification; validation asks whether it meets the user’s real need.
Leaving version control until the final project.
Thinking agile means no planning or no documentation.
Ignoring non-functional requirements such as security, performance and usability.
Starting the capstone late and leaving no time for testing and writing.

keyPoints: Software engineering applies engineering discipline to the whole life of software, not only to writing code.
Degree length, awards and accreditation differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Foundations in programming, mathematics and data structures come before process, design, testing and management topics.
Testing, version control and small complete projects teach more than reading alone.
Verification checks the specification; validation checks the real need.
Start the capstone early and keep evidence of your process, tests and decisions.

en.title: Introduction to software engineering
en.short: What software engineering is, software products, stakeholders, lifecycle, the software crisis and ethics.

sections.heading: Engineering, not just programming
sections.text: Software engineering is the application of a systematic, disciplined and measurable approach to developing, operating and maintaining software. Programming is writing code. Software engineering includes programming, but also planning, requirements, design, testing, maintenance, teamwork, cost and risk. It treats software as an engineered product, not a private craft.

sections.heading: Products and stakeholders
sections.text:
A software product is the software plus its documentation and data, built for users or for a market. A stakeholder is anyone who affects or is affected by the product: users, customers, developers, maintainers, funders and regulators.

Case: Amina manages a clinic in Kano and asks a team to build a patient records system. The nurses, doctors, records clerks, patients, funder and ministry are stakeholders. Coding is one task; the team must also agree requirements, protect patient data, test the system, train users and plan maintenance.

sections.heading: Lifecycle and crisis
sections.text:
The software lifecycle is the set of activities from the first idea to retirement. Common phases are requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. They often overlap and repeat.

The term software crisis was used from the late 1960s for large projects that ran late, cost too much or failed. It is linked to the 1968 NATO conference on software engineering. The response was to apply engineering discipline: plan work, define quality, review results and manage risk.

sections.heading: Ethics and practice
sections.text: Professional ethics covers honesty, competence, confidentiality, respect for privacy and avoiding harm. Professional bodies such as the ACM and the IEEE Computer Society publish codes of ethics. Regulation differs by country; for example, Nigeria has the Computer Professionals Registration Council of Nigeria (CPN). Professional practice also means documenting work, keeping skills current and reporting problems honestly.

keyPoints: Software engineering applies systematic, disciplined work to the whole software lifecycle, not only coding.
A software product includes the program, documentation and data, and serves users or a market.
A stakeholder is anyone affected by a product, including users, customers, developers and regulators.
The software crisis was the name given to widespread project failure in the late 1960s, and it led to engineering discipline.
Main lifecycle phases are requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance, and they often repeat.
Professional ethics requires honesty, competence, confidentiality and care for users and the public.

en.title: Programming fundamentals for software engineering
en.short: Variables, data types, expressions, control flow, functions and modular structure, plus reading, debugging and testing.

sections.heading: Values and types
sections.text:
A variable is a named storage location whose value can change. A data type says what kind of value it holds, such as integer, real, string or Boolean, and what operations are allowed. Declaring a type helps the system catch mistakes. An expression combines values and operators to produce a new value; for example, price × quantity. An assignment such as total = price × quantity stores the result in a variable.

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction unless brackets change the order. Integer division can surprise beginners: in many languages 7 ÷ 2 gives 3, not 3.5, when both operands are integers.

sections.heading: Control and functions
sections.text:
Control flow decides which statements run. A conditional (if, else) chooses a branch; a loop (while, for) repeats statements while a condition holds. Every loop needs a condition that eventually becomes false, or it may run forever. A function is a named block that takes inputs, called parameters or arguments, performs a task and may return a value. Functions remove repetition and give names to ideas.

For example, average(a, b) returns (a + b) ÷ 2. With a = 8 and b = 14, average returns 11. A modular program is split into small functions and files, each with one clear job and a simple interface.

sections.heading: Reading and debugging
sections.text:
To read a program, start at the entry point and trace values line by line. Write small programs first: read input, compute, print output. Debugging means finding and fixing defects. Reproduce the fault with the smallest input you can, inspect intermediate values, and form a hypothesis before editing.

A debugger lets you pause execution and step through statements. Print statements can also show values. Fix one cause at a time and rerun the same case.

sections.heading: Testing and clarity
sections.text:
Testing checks that code behaves as intended. A test case has an input and the expected output. Test normal cases, boundary cases and invalid input. For average(8, 14), expect 11. For average(0, 0), expect 0.

Clarity supports correctness: use meaningful names, keep functions short, avoid hidden global state, and comment why rather than what. Modular structure lets you test one function alone and replace it safely.

keyPoints: Variables are named storage locations; data types define the values and operations allowed.
Expressions combine values with operators, and brackets control precedence.
Control flow uses conditions and loops; every loop must terminate.
Functions take inputs, may return a value, and make programs modular.
Debug by reproducing the fault, inspecting values and changing one cause at a time.
Test normal, boundary and invalid cases, and keep code clear with meaningful names.

en.title: Discrete mathematics for software engineering
en.short: Logic, sets, relations, functions, graphs, counting and induction, with their use in software.

sections.heading: Logic and specifications
sections.text: Propositional logic builds statements from atomic propositions using AND, OR, NOT and IMPLIES. A truth table lists every combination of truth values. Predicate logic adds variables, predicates and quantifiers: for all and there exists. It can say that every order has a customer. These ideas support specifications: a precondition states what must hold before an operation, and a postcondition states what must hold after it. They also support testing, because test cases can make each condition true and false.

sections.heading: Sets, relations and databases
sections.text: A set is a collection of distinct objects. Operations include union, intersection and difference. A relation is a set of ordered pairs, such as (customer, order). In a relational database, a table is a relation: a set of rows over named columns. Keys and foreign keys are constraints on relations. A function is a special relation that maps each input to exactly one output. Functions model calculations, lookups and mappings between identifiers.

sections.heading: Graphs and algorithms
sections.text: A graph has vertices and edges. Directed graphs model dependencies, state machines and task orders; undirected graphs model symmetric links. Graph algorithms answer reachability, shortest path and cycle questions. Algorithm reasoning uses invariants, conditions that stay true at each step, and complexity bounds. A loop invariant can show that a search returns the correct index.

sections.heading: Counting and induction
sections.text: Counting uses the product rule, the sum rule and combinations. The number of ways to choose 2 testers from 5 is C(5,2) = 5! ÷ (2! × 3!) = 10. This helps estimate test effort and count possible inputs. Proof by induction has a base case and an inductive step. To prove 1 + 3 + ... + (2n − 1) = n², the base n = 1 gives 1 = 1². Assume it for k; adding the next odd number gives k² + (2k + 1) = (k + 1)². Induction supports reasoning about loops and recursive algorithms.

keyPoints: Propositional logic uses AND, OR, NOT and IMPLIES; predicate logic adds for all and there exists.
Sets support unions, intersections and database relations; functions map each input to exactly one output.
Graphs model dependencies and networks, and graph algorithms answer reachability and shortest path questions.
Counting uses the product rule, sum rule and combinations; C(5,2) = 10.
Proof by induction has a base case and an inductive step.
Invariants and complexity bounds support reasoning about algorithms.

en.title: Data structures and algorithms
en.short: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, hash tables, searching, sorting and asymptotic cost.

sections.heading: Arrays and linked lists
sections.text:
An array stores items in contiguous memory with index. Reading or writing a[i] takes O(1) time. Inserting or deleting in the middle takes O(n) time because later items shift. A linked list stores each item in a node with a pointer to the next node. Finding the kth item takes O(n) time, but inserting or deleting at a node you already hold takes O(1) time.

Example: inserting at the front of a 1,000-item array shifts 1,000 items; a linked list changes two pointers.

sections.heading: Stacks queues hash tables
sections.text:
A stack is last in, first out: push adds and pop removes at the top, both O(1). A queue is first in, first out: enqueue adds at the back and dequeue removes at the front, both O(1).

A hash table maps a key to a bucket with a hash function. Average lookup, insert and delete are O(1); worst case is O(n) when many keys collide. Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing.

sections.heading: Trees searching sorting
sections.text:
A tree has nodes with parent and child links. In a binary search tree, left values are smaller and right values larger. Search, insert and delete take O(log n) time when balanced, but O(n) when the tree becomes a chain. Linear search checks items in turn and takes O(n). Binary search needs sorted data and takes O(log n).

Example: search for 42 in [3, 8, 15, 23, 42, 57, 61, 75]. Compare with index 3 value 23, go right; index 5 value 57, go left; index 4 value 42, found in three comparisons.

Sorting puts items in order. Insertion sort takes O(n²) worst case. Merge sort takes O(n log n) in all cases and needs extra memory. Quicksort averages O(n log n) but has an O(n²) worst case. Asymptotic complexity describes how cost grows with input size n: O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound, and Θ a tight bound. Choose a structure by the operations you need most, and design algorithms by dividing problems into smaller parts.

keyPoints: Array index access is O(1), but inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n).
Linked list access is O(n), but inserting or deleting at a known node is O(1).
Stack is LIFO and queue is FIFO; their push, pop, enqueue and dequeue operations are O(1).
Hash table average lookup is O(1), but worst case is O(n) when collisions are many.
Binary search needs sorted data and takes O(log n); linear search takes O(n).
Merge sort is O(n log n) in all cases; quicksort averages O(n log n) with O(n²) worst case; O is an upper bound, Ω a lower bound and Θ a tight bound.

en.title: Object-oriented programming and modelling
en.short: Classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, and UML class and use case diagrams.

sections.heading: Classes and objects
sections.text: A class is a blueprint that groups data (attributes) and behaviour (methods). An object is one instance of a class, with its own attribute values. In a simple library system, class Book has attributes title and borrowed, and methods borrow() and returnBook(). Two objects, bookA and bookB, share the methods but hold different titles and states. Calling bookA.borrow() changes only bookA.

sections.heading: Encapsulation and inheritance
sections.text: Encapsulation hides an object’s internal state behind methods, so other code cannot change it directly. The class exposes a public operation and keeps its fields private, protecting rules such as 'a book cannot be borrowed twice'. Inheritance lets a class reuse and extend another. A Member and a Librarian may both inherit from Person, gaining name and email while adding their own behaviour. Inheritance models an is-a relationship; use it only when that sentence is true.

sections.heading: Polymorphism and interfaces
sections.text: Polymorphism means one operation can behave differently for different classes. If Person has notify(), Member.notify() might send a loan reminder and Librarian.notify() a rota message; code can call notify() without knowing the exact class. An interface names a set of operations without giving their code. A class that implements Notifier promises to provide notify(). Interfaces let unrelated classes share a contract, and they support testing with substitutes.

sections.heading: Modelling with UML
sections.text: UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagrams show classes, attributes, methods and relationships: association, inheritance (a hollow triangle) and interface realisation (a dashed line with a hollow triangle). A use case diagram shows actors outside the system and the use cases they take part in, such as Borrow book or Return book. These diagrams bridge code and design: the class diagram mirrors the code structure, while the use case diagram records what users need.

keyPoints: A class is a blueprint for objects; an object is one instance with its own state.
Encapsulation keeps fields private and exposes controlled methods.
Inheritance models an is-a relationship and lets a class reuse another.
Polymorphism lets one operation behave differently across classes.
An interface is a contract of operations that implementing classes must provide.
UML class diagrams show code structure; use case diagrams show actors and system functions.

en.title: Databases and SQL
en.short: This covers the relational model, keys, constraints, SQL queries and updates, normalisation and transactions.

sections.heading: Tables and keys
sections.text:
A database stores persistent data, which survives after the program stops. In the relational model, data sits in relations, seen as tables. Each row is a tuple; each column is an attribute. Rows are unique and column order does not matter.

A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. The chosen one is the primary key, which cannot be null. A foreign key refers to a primary key in another table.

sections.heading: SQL and constraints
sections.text:
Integrity constraints are rules the database enforces. Entity integrity says a primary key is unique and not null. Referential integrity says a foreign key must match an existing primary key, or be null. UNIQUE, NOT NULL and CHECK are other constraints.

SQL is the standard language for queries and updates. Queries use SELECT, FROM and WHERE; updates use INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. Dialects differ, so check your database manual.

Example: Student(id, name, score) holds (1, Ada, 70), (2, Bola, 55), (3, Chidi, 55).
SELECT name FROM Student WHERE score >= 60; returns Ada.
UPDATE Student SET score = score + 5 WHERE score < 60; makes Bola and Chidi 60.

sections.heading: Normalisation
sections.text:
Normalisation removes redundancy and update anomalies. First normal form (1NF) requires atomic values and no repeating groups. Second normal form (2NF) removes partial dependencies on part of a composite key. Third normal form (3NF) removes transitive dependencies, where a non-key column depends on another non-key column.

Example: Orders(OrderID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress) repeats the address. Split it into Orders(OrderID, CustomerID) and Customers(CustomerID, Name, Address). This is 3NF and avoids inconsistent addresses.

sections.heading: Transactions
sections.text:
A transaction is a group of operations that must succeed or fail as one unit. ACID means atomicity (all or nothing), consistency (rules preserved), isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere) and durability (committed changes survive failure).

Example: moving 100 naira from account A to B runs two updates. If the second fails, ROLLBACK undoes the first. COMMIT saves the work.

keyPoints: A relation is a table with unique rows; a primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be null.
A foreign key links to a primary key in another table and enforces referential integrity.
SQL uses SELECT for queries and INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for changes.
Normalisation reduces redundancy: 1NF atomic values, 2NF no partial dependencies, 3NF no transitive dependencies.
A transaction groups operations and follows ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability.
COMMIT saves a transaction; ROLLBACK cancels it.

en.title: Computer systems and networks for software
en.short: CPU, memory, OS, IP, TCP, UDP, DNS, HTTP and client-server deployment choices.

sections.heading: Processor and memory
sections.text: The CPU (central processing unit) runs instructions in a fetch-decode-execute cycle. Registers hold current data; cores let several instruction streams run at once. Memory (RAM) holds running programs and data, is fast and volatile, so it loses content when power goes. Storage (SSD or hard disk) is slower and keeps data without power. A program becomes a process when the OS loads it into memory.

sections.heading: Operating system
sections.text: The operating system (OS) manages CPU time, memory and devices. It schedules processes, giving each a share of the CPU, and uses virtual memory to give each process its own address space. A file is named, persistent data managed by the file system. The OS maps file names to disk blocks and enforces permissions. Example: saving notes.txt asks the OS to write bytes into free disk blocks.

sections.heading: Network layers
sections.text: Networks are described in layers. In TCP/IP, the link layer moves frames on one network, the internet layer routes packets with IP addresses, the transport layer moves data between programs, and the application layer holds protocols such as DNS and HTTP. An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers, for example 192.168.1.10. With a /24 mask, 192.168.1.0 is the network, .1 to .254 are hosts and .255 is broadcast. TCP is reliable and ordered; UDP sends independent datagrams without guarantees. DNS maps names to IP addresses. HTTP is a request-response protocol, usually over TCP, carrying methods such as GET and POST.

sections.heading: Clients and deployment
sections.text: In client-server, a client sends requests and a server replies. A distant server adds latency, so caching or a closer region helps; stateless servers scale more easily; mobile clients need retries. A Nairobi campus app might cache data and use HTTPS to a cloud server. Deployment choices include on-premises, cloud, containers and content delivery networks. Each changes cost, scaling, failures and data location; check local rules.

keyPoints: The CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions; RAM is volatile working memory and storage is persistent.
The OS schedules processes, gives each a virtual address space, and manages files through the file system.
TCP/IP layers separate link, internet, transport and application concerns.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits; a /24 mask gives 254 usable host addresses on a small network.
TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is not, DNS resolves names, and HTTP carries web requests.
Client-server and deployment choices change latency, scaling, cost and failure behaviour.

en.title: Web and mobile foundations
en.short: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, HTTP APIs, responsive design and mobile app structure.

sections.heading: Pages, styles, scripts
sections.text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure of a page with elements such as headings, paragraphs and forms. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation: colour, spacing and layout. JavaScript adds behaviour: it can respond to taps, validate a form and change the page without reloading it. Keep the three separate. A page that works without JavaScript, and with clear labels on inputs, is easier to use and to maintain.

sections.heading: Browser, server and APIs
sections.text:
A browser sends an HTTP request to a server and receives a response. GET asks for a resource; POST sends data. The status code says what happened: 200 means OK, 404 means not found, 500 means server error. An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for programs to talk. A web API often returns JSON, a text format of keys and values.

HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone. A session lets the server remember a user across requests, usually by a cookie holding a session identifier. Treat that identifier as secret and use HTTPS.

sections.heading: Responsive design
sections.text: Responsive design makes one page usable on many screen sizes. Start with a viewport meta tag so the phone uses its real width. Use fluid grids with relative units such as % and rem (relative to the root font size), flexible images, and media queries that change layout at set widths. Design mobile first: the small layout is the base, and wider screens add columns.

sections.heading: Mobile structure and limits
sections.text: A mobile app is organised into screens with a navigation path, shared state and local storage. Phones have less memory and slower processors than laptops, and battery life is limited. Networks may be slow, costly or absent, so cache data and handle failure. Touch targets need enough size. Example: a student opens a results app. It sends GET /api/results with the session cookie, receives 200 and JSON, caches it, and shows a clear message if the phone is offline.

keyPoints: HTML gives structure, CSS gives presentation and JavaScript gives behaviour.
HTTP requests carry a method, responses carry a status code, and both often carry JSON.
HTTP is stateless; sessions use a cookie identifier to link requests.
Responsive design uses a viewport tag, fluid units and media queries.
Mobile devices constrain memory, battery, network and screen size, so cache and handle failure.
Keep the session identifier secret and serve apps over HTTPS.

en.title: Software tools and version control
en.short: IDEs, build tools, package managers, Git workflows, issue trackers and continuous integration.

sections.heading: IDE and build tools
sections.text:
An integrated development environment (IDE) combines an editor, compiler or interpreter, debugger and file browser. It helps you write and run code, but learn the underlying commands too.

A build system turns source files into a runnable program and repeats the steps the same way each time. Examples are Make, Maven and Gradle. A package manager installs and updates reusable libraries, such as pip for Python or npm for JavaScript, and records them in a manifest file so another machine can rebuild the same setup.

sections.heading: Git basics
sections.text:
Git is a distributed version control system: every clone holds the full history. A repository is the project plus its history. A commit is a saved snapshot with a message, author and time. A branch is a movable line of work; main or master is only a convention.

A merge joins branches. If both changed the same lines, Git reports a conflict and you edit the file, then commit the resolution. A simple workflow is: pull, create a branch, commit small changes, push, open a pull request, review, merge. A pull request asks others to review a branch before merging. Commit often, with clear messages, so history is useful.

sections.heading: Issues, tests and CI
sections.text:
An issue tracker records bugs, tasks and feature requests with owners and status. An automated test runner runs your test suite and reports pass or fail; examples are pytest and JUnit.

Continuous integration (CI) means a server builds the code and runs tests after each push. Case: Amina pushes a branch; CI runs the build and tests. A failing test blocks the merge until she fixes it. This catches integration mistakes early. CI should run quickly and use a clean environment, so results are repeatable.

keyPoints: An IDE combines editing, running and debugging tools; a build system repeats compilation steps.
A package manager installs libraries and records versions in a manifest.
Git stores snapshots as commits; branches let you work separately and merges combine work.
Resolve a merge conflict by editing the marked files and committing the result.
Issue trackers record work; automated test runners report pass or fail.
CI builds and tests every push, catching integration errors early.

en.title: Software process models
en.short: Compares waterfall, V-model, incremental, iterative and spiral lifecycles, with deliverables, risk and selection criteria.

sections.heading: What models do
sections.text: A process model is a simplified structure for the activities, roles and deliverables of software work. A deliverable is a tangible output, such as a specification, design document, test report or working release. A risk profile describes which problems are likely and how costly they are to fix late. Every model covers requirements, design, construction, testing, delivery and maintenance, but arranges them differently.

sections.heading: Waterfall and V
sections.text: Waterfall runs requirements, design, construction, testing and maintenance in sequence. Deliverables include a requirements specification, design documents, code, test reports and a maintained system. Its risk is late feedback: misunderstood requirements are costly to change. The V-model keeps the sequence but pairs each development phase with a test level. Requirements pair with acceptance testing, design with system and integration testing, and module design with unit testing. Test plans are early deliverables. It finds defects sooner but remains weak when requirements change often.

sections.heading: Incremental and iterative
sections.text: Incremental delivery builds usable subsets of the system. Each increment passes through requirements, design, construction and testing; its deliverable is a working release. Its risk is poor integration or weak early architecture. Iterative development repeats cycles to refine the system; deliverables are evolving releases or prototypes. It lowers requirements risk through feedback but can drift without clear scope. Spiral is risk-driven: each loop sets objectives, analyses risk, engineers a solution and evaluates it. Deliverables include prototypes and risk assessments. It suits large, high-risk projects but is costly to manage.

sections.heading: Choosing a model
sections.text: Choose by requirements stability, scale, regulation and team context. Stable, well-understood requirements with documentation suit waterfall or V. Unstable requirements suit iterative or incremental work. Large, high-risk systems suit spiral. Regulation may require traceability and records, so test plans and approvals matter. Team experience, customer availability and distribution shape the choice. Case: a Ghanaian clinic system has fixed audit rules but growing modules. The team uses incremental delivery, agreeing acceptance tests per module, so audit evidence exists and users see value early.

keyPoints: Waterfall is sequential and suits stable requirements but makes late change expensive.
The V-model pairs each development phase with a matching test level.
Incremental delivery produces working releases in usable subsets and needs strong architecture.
Iterative cycles reduce requirements risk through feedback but need scope control.
Spiral is risk-driven and suits large, high-risk projects at higher management cost.
Process choice depends on requirements stability, scale, regulation and team context.

en.title: Agile and lean software development
en.short: Agile values, Scrum, XP, Kanban, user stories, estimation, retrospectives and limits.

sections.heading: Agile values
sections.text: Agile is a set of values and principles, not one method. The Agile Manifesto (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. It does not reject the right-hand items; it weights the left more. Its principles favour frequent delivery, welcoming changing requirements, self-organising teams, technical excellence and regular reflection. Lean adds removing waste, limiting work in progress and improving the whole flow.

sections.heading: Scrum
sections.text: Scrum has three accountabilities: the Product Owner orders the product backlog; the Scrum Master helps the team apply Scrum and removes impediments; the Developers build the increment. The events are Sprint Planning, the Daily Scrum, the Sprint Review and the Sprint Retrospective. A sprint is a fixed timebox. The product backlog, sprint backlog and increment make work visible. The team delivers a usable increment each sprint and inspects it with stakeholders.

sections.heading: XP and Kanban
sections.text: Extreme Programming (XP) is an engineering-centred agile method. Practices include pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases, simple design, refactoring, collective code ownership and an on-site customer. Kanban is a flow method: visualise the workflow, limit work in progress (WIP), manage flow, make policies explicit and improve collaboratively. Unlike Scrum, Kanban usually has no fixed sprint or prescribed roles; it suits interrupt-driven work such as support.

sections.heading: Stories, planning, limits
sections.text: User stories are needs written as: As a role, I want a goal so that a benefit. Teams prioritise by value, risk and cost, using methods such as MoSCoW (must, should, could, won’t). Estimation is relative: teams size items in story points, often using planning poker, where each member picks a card in secret and all reveal together, then discuss until they agree. Velocity is the average points completed per sprint. Do not convert points to hours. A retrospective asks what went well, what did not, and what to change. Agile has limits: safety-critical, regulated or fixed-price work may need more up-front documentation and formal verification; distributed teams and weak customer access reduce its benefits.

keyPoints: Agile values working software, collaboration and response to change over documentation, contracts and plans, while still respecting them.
Scrum uses Product Owner, Scrum Master and Developers, with Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
XP stresses engineering practices such as pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration and refactoring.
Kanban visualises flow and limits work in progress; it does not require fixed sprints.
User stories express needs from a user role; story points estimate relative size, not hours.
Agile works best with access to customers and room to change scope; regulated or fixed-price settings may need more formal documentation.

en.title: Requirements engineering
en.short: Elicitation, analysis, SRS, use cases, functional and non-functional requirements, validation and traceability.

sections.heading: Elicitation and analysis
sections.text:
Requirements engineering is the disciplined process of finding, agreeing, writing and controlling what a software system must do. Elicitation gathers needs from stakeholders, the people affected by the system. Useful techniques are interviews, workshops, observation, questionnaires and prototypes. Analysis checks raw needs for conflicts, gaps, feasibility and cost, and negotiates priorities.

For example, Amina runs a Kano clinic. Patients want SMS reminders, but there is no SMS budget, so the team agrees on email reminders and printed slips.

sections.heading: Functional and non-functional
sections.text: A functional requirement states a service or behaviour, such as the system shall let a patient book an appointment. A non-functional requirement states a quality or constraint, such as response time, security, availability, usability or a legal rule. Good non-functional requirements are measurable: 95 percent of booking requests shall be confirmed within 2 seconds. Vague words like fast cannot be tested. Constraints, such as using the clinic’s existing database, are also recorded.

sections.heading: Specification and use cases
sections.text: The specification is the agreed written record. A software requirements specification, SRS, covers purpose and scope, users, functional requirements, non-functional requirements, interfaces, constraints and acceptance criteria. Standards such as ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 give guidance, not a fixed template. A use case describes one goal from an actor’s point of view, where an actor is a person or another system that interacts with the software. It lists the actor, goal, preconditions, main flow, alternative flows and postconditions. For booking, the actor is the patient, the goal is to book a slot, and an alternative flow handles a full clinic.

sections.heading: Validation and management
sections.text: Validation asks whether requirements are correct, complete, consistent and testable. Reviews, prototypes and acceptance tests with users expose misunderstandings. Management keeps requirements under control after the baseline, the agreed and fixed set of requirements: give each an identifier, record its source, set a priority, and use change control and versioning. Traceability links each requirement forward to design, code and tests, and backward to its source. A traceability matrix makes gaps visible, such as a requirement with no test or code with no requirement.

keyPoints: Elicitation gathers stakeholder needs; analysis resolves conflicts, gaps and priorities.
Functional requirements state services; non-functional requirements state measurable qualities or constraints.
An SRS records scope, users, requirements, interfaces, constraints and acceptance criteria.
A use case describes an actor’s goal with preconditions, main flow, alternatives and postconditions.
Validation checks that requirements are correct, complete, consistent and testable.
Traceability links requirements to sources, design, code and tests, and change control keeps the baseline under management.

en.title: System modelling and UML
en.short: UML structure and behaviour diagrams, and how to keep the views consistent.

sections.heading: Structural views
sections.text: A model is an abstraction of a system, built to explain it and to check decisions before code exists. UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a standard notation maintained by the Object Management Group. Class diagrams show classes, attributes, operations, associations and multiplicities, such as one Student borrowing many Books. Component diagrams show replaceable parts and the interfaces they provide or require. Deployment diagrams show nodes, such as servers or phones, and the artefacts placed on them.

sections.heading: Behavioural views
sections.text: Use case diagrams show actors outside the system and the goals, called use cases, that they pursue. They give scope, not a sequence of steps. Activity diagrams show workflows with decisions, forks and joins. State machine diagrams show the states of one object and the events that move it between states. Sequence diagrams show interactions over time: lifelines, messages and returns. Together these views describe what the system does and when.

sections.heading: Keeping views consistent
sections.text: Each diagram is a view of one underlying model. Use the same names for the same element in every view, and link related elements by traceability. A use case should lead to classes and operations; a sequence message should name an operation on a class; a state should be consistent with the class’s attributes. Review changes across views, and keep the model in a shared repository so that one edit does not leave two conflicting versions.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text: Consider a library loan system. The use case Borrow book has actor Student. The class diagram has Student, Book, Loan and Library, with Loan linking one Student to one Book. A sequence diagram for Borrow book sends borrow(book) from Student to Library, then createLoan() from Library to Loan. A state machine for Book moves Available to On loan on borrow, and back on return. A component diagram shows a LoanService providing a Loan interface. A deployment diagram places LoanService on an application server and the database on a database server.

keyPoints: UML is a standard notation, not a method or a process.
Class, component and deployment diagrams show structure; use case, activity, state machine and sequence diagrams show behaviour.
Use case diagrams define system scope through actors and goals, not message order.
Sequence diagrams show interactions over time; state machine diagrams show one object’s states and transitions.
Keep one underlying model: reuse names, trace links and review across views.
Consistency checks include matching use cases to classes, messages to operations and states to attribute values.

en.title: Software architecture: structure, styles and trade-offs
en.short: High-level structure, views, common styles, quality trade-offs and simple architecture descriptions.

sections.heading: Architecture and design
sections.text: Architecture is the set of high-level design decisions about a system’s structure: its main components, how they connect, and the constraints that shape them. It is part of design, not a separate phase. Detailed design fills in classes and algorithms; architecture sets the frame those details must fit. Good architecture records why decisions were made, because that rationale guides change.

sections.heading: Views and styles
sections.text: A view describes one concern; no single diagram shows everything. Common styles: layered puts components in layers, each using only the layer below, which supports replaceability but can add overhead. Client-server has clients request services from servers, centralising data but risking the server as a bottleneck. Pipe-and-filter passes data through filters linked by pipes, good for streams and reuse. MVC splits model (data and rules), view (display) and controller (input), so the interface can change without rewriting the model.

sections.heading: Quality attributes and trade-offs
sections.text: Quality attributes are measurable non-functional properties such as performance, availability, security, modifiability and testability. Architecture strongly affects them. A trade-off means improving one may weaken another: caching improves response time but can show stale data; layering improves modifiability but may cost performance. Example: a university results portal in Lagos, built by Ada and Tunde, uses client-server for central records. Adding a cache helps peak results day but needs a rule for when marks change.

sections.heading: Describing an architecture
sections.text: A simple architecture description names components, their responsibilities, connectors, constraints and key rationale. A box-and-line diagram alone is weak; add a short table or text: component, responsibility, connector. For the portal: web client (displays results) connects by HTTPS to results server (checks permissions and fetches marks), which sends SQL queries to the database (stores records). State constraints such as 'only the server accesses the database' and the reason. This is enough for review before detailed design.

keyPoints: Architecture is the high-level structure of components, connectors and constraints, and it is part of design rather than a separate phase.
Use several views, such as logical, process and deployment, because one diagram cannot show every concern.
Layered, client-server, pipe-and-filter and MVC are common styles with different strengths and costs.
Quality attributes such as performance, security and modifiability are shaped by architecture and often trade off against each other.
A useful architecture description states components, responsibilities, connectors, constraints and rationale, not just boxes and lines.

en.title: Design principles and patterns
en.short: Modularity, coupling, cohesion, SOLID and GRASP, and when GoF patterns help or harm.

sections.heading: Modules and dependencies
sections.text:
Modularity means splitting a system into parts that can be understood and changed separately. Coupling is how much one module depends on another; loose coupling is easier to change. Cohesion is how strongly the parts of one module belong together; high cohesion is easier to understand. Information hiding means a module exposes only what callers need and keeps its internals private, so changes stay local.

Case: Amina builds a results portal. If the report page reads the database directly, a schema change breaks it. Putting database access behind a small interface reduces coupling.

sections.heading: SOLID principles
sections.text:
SOLID is five object-oriented design principles. Single responsibility: a class should have one reason to change. Open/closed: open to extension, closed to modification. Liskov substitution: subtypes must work wherever the parent type is expected. Interface segregation: many small interfaces beat one large one. Dependency inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete details.

GRASP (General Responsibility Assignment Software Patterns) gives responsibility-assignment advice: Information Expert, Creator, Controller, Low Coupling, High Cohesion, Polymorphism, Pure Fabrication, Indirection and Protected Variations. Use it to decide which class should do a job.

sections.heading: GoF patterns
sections.text:
The Gang of Four book, Design Patterns (1994), groups patterns as creational, structural and behavioural. Factory Method hides which class is created. Adapter converts one interface to another. Observer lets objects subscribe to changes. Strategy swaps algorithms behind one interface.

Patterns help by naming a proven design and giving a shared vocabulary. They harm when applied before the need is clear: extra classes, indirection and coupling can make a small system harder to maintain. Apply a pattern when a real variation point exists, not because the pattern is famous.

keyPoints: Modularity splits a system into parts that can change independently.
Aim for low coupling and high cohesion, and hide internal details.
SOLID covers single responsibility, open/closed, Liskov, interface segregation and dependency inversion.
GRASP assigns responsibilities using Information Expert, Low Coupling, High Cohesion and related patterns.
GoF patterns are reusable designs grouped as creational, structural and behavioural.
Patterns help communication and reuse but add complexity if used without a real need.

en.title: Software construction and code quality
en.short: Coding standards, naming, comments, defensive code, review, refactoring, static analysis and technical debt.

sections.heading: Standards and names
sections.text:
Coding standards are a team’s agreed rules for layout, naming, error handling and file structure. They make code predictable, so a reader can find things without guessing.

Good names state intent: calculateMonthlyFee is clearer than calc. Keep abbreviations rare and follow the codebase convention. A standard helps only if the team writes it down and applies it in review.

sections.heading: Comments and defence
sections.text:
Comments explain why, not what. Update them when behaviour changes; a wrong comment is worse than none.

Defensive programming assumes inputs and other systems can fail. Validate arguments at boundaries, check return values, fail fast with a clear error, and avoid silent defaults.

Amina and Chidi build a school fees system in Kano, Nigeria. A function p(amount) accepts any value. Review asks for payFees(studentId, amountKobo) and a check that amountKobo > 0. The guard takes minutes and prevents bad records.

sections.heading: Review and analysis
sections.text:
Code review is a planned reading of a change by another developer before it is merged. It catches defects early, spreads knowledge and checks standards. Keep reviews small and focused on correctness, clarity and risk.

Static analysis uses tools that read source code without running it. They flag unused variables, risky patterns and possible null dereferences. Tools produce false positives, so treat findings as questions, not verdicts. People judge design; tools check rules.

sections.heading: Refactoring and debt
sections.text:
Refactoring changes internal structure without changing observable behaviour. Rename a variable, split a long function, remove duplication, then rerun tests.

Technical debt is the future cost of a shortcut taken now. Some debt is sensible, such as shipping a simple version early; much is accidental, such as unclear names and missing checks. Debt grows with interest: each later change takes longer. Construction choices decide whether maintenance is cheap or painful. Record known debt and repay it before it blocks change.

keyPoints: Agree coding standards and use intention-revealing names so code is predictable.
Comments should explain why, and must be updated when behaviour changes.
Defensive programming validates inputs at boundaries and fails fast with clear errors.
Code review catches defects early and spreads knowledge; keep changes small.
Static analysis finds some defects without running code, but its warnings need judgement.
Technical debt is future cost; refactor in small steps and record debt before it slows maintenance.

en.title: Software testing fundamentals
en.short: Verification and validation, test levels, black-box and white-box methods, coverage and oracles.

sections.heading: Verification and validation
sections.text: Verification asks whether the software conforms to its specification: are we building the product right? Validation asks whether it meets the user’s real needs: are we building the right product? Verification includes reviews, inspections and tests against requirements. Validation includes acceptance testing and use in realistic conditions. A product can pass verification and still fail validation if the specification itself is wrong.

sections.heading: Test levels
sections.text: Unit testing checks one component, such as a function or class, often with stubs, simple stand-ins for the real dependencies. Integration testing checks how components work together and exposes interface and data-flow faults. System testing checks the whole system against requirements in an environment close to production. Acceptance testing is done by or for the customer to decide whether to accept the system; it may be user acceptance, alpha or beta testing. Each level needs a test oracle, the source of expected results, such as a specification or a user’s judgement.

sections.heading: Black and white box
sections.text: Black-box testing derives tests from the specification without seeing the code. Equivalence partitioning divides inputs into classes treated alike, then tests one value from each class. Boundary value analysis tests values at, just inside and just outside the edges of each class, where faults often cluster. White-box testing derives tests from code structure, such as statements, branches and paths. It can find unreachable code and untested branches, but it cannot detect required behaviour that is missing from the code.

sections.heading: Coverage and oracles
sections.text: Coverage measures how much of a chosen structure tests exercise: statement coverage counts executed statements, branch coverage counts taken branches, and path coverage counts executed paths. High coverage is evidence, not proof, of correctness. A test oracle is the source of expected results. For an age field accepted from 18 to 65, equivalence classes are below 18, 18 to 65, and above 65. Boundary tests are 17, 18, 19, 64, 65 and 66. If a suite executes 45 of 50 statements, statement coverage is 45 ÷ 50 = 90 per cent.

keyPoints: Verification checks conformance to specification; validation checks that the product meets real user needs.
Unit, integration, system and acceptance testing answer different questions at different levels.
Black-box tests come from the specification; white-box tests come from code structure.
Equivalence partitioning tests one value per input class; boundary value analysis tests edges.
Statement coverage = executed statements ÷ total statements × 100%; high coverage does not prove correctness.
A test oracle is the source of expected results, such as a specification, model or user judgement.

en.title: Automated testing and continuous integration
en.short: Unit test frameworks, test doubles, TDD, regression suites, CI pipelines, flaky tests and maintainability.

sections.heading: Unit tests and frameworks
sections.text:
A unit test checks one small behaviour of a function or class in isolation. A unit test framework supplies a test runner that finds and runs tests, assertions that compare actual and expected values, and a pass or fail report. Good unit tests are fast, deterministic and independent.

Example: Amina tests a delivery fee function. For an order of 2,000 at 25 percent, the assertion expects 500. The test fails until the function returns 500.

sections.heading: Doubles and TDD
sections.text:
Test doubles replace real collaborators so a unit can be tested alone. A stub returns fixed answers, a fake is a simple working substitute, and a mock records calls and checks expectations. Use doubles at boundaries; too many mocks make tests brittle.

Test-driven development (TDD) is a short cycle: write a failing test for the next behaviour (red), write the simplest code that passes (green), then improve the design without changing behaviour (refactor). The tests become a regression suite: tests rerun after every change to catch behaviour that breaks.

sections.heading: Continuous integration
sections.text:
Continuous integration (CI) means merging small changes into a shared main line often, with a pipeline that builds and tests each change automatically. A pipeline is a scripted sequence: fetch the code, install dependencies, build, run unit and integration tests, and publish a report. A failed step stops the pipeline and notifies the team, so a broken change is found within minutes.

A CI service runs the pipeline on a clean machine. Keep it fast; run the full regression suite before merging.

sections.heading: Flaky tests and upkeep
sections.text:
A flaky test sometimes passes and sometimes fails. Common causes are timing, shared state, network access and dependence on the current date or random values. Fix or quarantine flaky tests, meaning skip or flag them so they do not block the build; teams stop trusting a red build.

Maintainability means the suite stays easy to change. Keep tests small and readable, test behaviour rather than private details, and delete tests that no longer express a requirement. A slow, brittle suite costs more than a clear, fast one.

keyPoints: Unit tests check small behaviours in isolation and should be fast and deterministic.
Test doubles replace collaborators; stubs return values, fakes work simply, mocks check calls.
TDD follows red, green, refactor and turns tests into a regression suite.
A CI pipeline builds, tests and reports on every change, usually on a clean machine.
Flaky tests pass and fail without code changes and must be fixed or quarantined.
Maintainable test suites stay small, readable and focused on behaviour.

en.title: Software verification and validation
en.short: Reviews, inspections, static analysis and formal methods as complementary evidence for acceptance.

sections.heading: Verification and validation
sections.text: Verification asks whether a product meets its specified requirements: are we building it right? Validation asks whether it meets the user’s real need: are we building the right product? Both are assurance activities. Testing executes software; reviews, static analysis and formal methods examine artefacts without running them. They are complementary because each finds different defects.

sections.heading: Reviews and inspections
sections.text:
Reviews are structured examinations by people. A walkthrough is informal, led by the author. A technical review uses a small team and recorded findings. An inspection is a formal review with defined roles, entry criteria, a checklist, and follow-up. Inspections can find requirement, design and code defects early, when repair is cheap.

Case: a team in Kano reviews a payroll module before release. A checklist item asks how overtime is rounded. The reviewer finds that the specification says round down but the code rounds up. The defect is fixed before testing, saving a later acceptance failure.

sections.heading: Analysis and formal methods
sections.text:
Static analysis examines source code or models without executing them. It includes type checking, linting, control-flow and data-flow analysis, and checks for risky patterns such as null dereferences or unreachable code. Tools report possible defects; people must judge false positives.

Formal methods use mathematical models to specify or prove properties. Model checking explores states; theorem proving shows that a design satisfies a property. They give strong evidence for critical parts, but need expertise and can be costly, so they complement, not replace, other assurance.

sections.heading: Evidence and acceptance
sections.text:
Assurance evidence comes from testing, review and analysis. A test shows that a case passed, not that no faults remain. Reviews and analysis cover things tests may miss. Acceptance should use planned criteria, traceability from requirements to evidence, and risk: critical functions need stronger evidence.

Confidence grows when independent evidence agrees. It is a judgement, not a guarantee.

keyPoints: Verification checks conformance to the specification; validation checks fitness for intended use.
Reviews range from informal walkthroughs to formal inspections with roles, checklists and follow-up.
Static analysis finds possible defects without executing code, but results need human judgement.
Formal methods such as model checking and theorem proving give strong evidence for critical properties but are costly and need expertise.
Testing can show that faults are present, not that none remain.
Acceptance should rest on planned criteria, traceability and risk-based evidence from testing, review and analysis.

en.title: Software maintenance and evolution
en.short: Corrective, adaptive, perfective, preventive maintenance, legacy systems, reengineering, technical debt, safe change.

sections.heading: Maintenance types
sections.text: Maintenance is work done after delivery to keep software useful. Corrective maintenance fixes defects found in use. Adaptive maintenance responds to changes outside the system, such as a new operating system or tax rule. Perfective maintenance improves behaviour that is already correct, for example speed or usability. Preventive maintenance reduces future trouble by refactoring, adding tests or updating dependencies. Evolution is the longer-term sequence of these changes as needs and technology move.

sections.heading: Legacy and reengineering
sections.text: A legacy system is old software that is still important but hard to change because it is large, undocumented or tied to old technology. Reverse engineering recovers design information from code and data; it does not change the system. Reengineering restructures or replaces parts while preserving required behaviour, often after reverse engineering. Rewriting from scratch is risky because hidden rules may be lost.

sections.heading: Technical debt and impact
sections.text: Technical debt is the future cost of a quick or poor design choice. Like money debt, it can be useful if repaid soon, but interest grows as changes become slower and riskier. Impact analysis predicts which requirements, modules, tests and users a proposed change will affect. It combines code search, dependency diagrams, test coverage and review by people who know the system. Good impact analysis limits unexpected breakage.

sections.heading: Safe change case
sections.text: Safe change means making evolution controlled. Use version control, small changes, automated tests, code review, staged release and a rollback plan. Case: Amina maintains a clinic records system in Kano, Nigeria. A new tax rule needs adaptive maintenance; a slow report needs perfective work; a crash needs corrective work; adding tests is preventive. Before changing the tax rule, she traces where totals are calculated, runs regression tests and releases to one clinic first. If errors appear, she rolls back.

keyPoints: Corrective maintenance fixes defects, adaptive maintenance responds to environment changes, perfective maintenance improves correct behaviour, and preventive maintenance reduces future cost.
Legacy systems are important but hard to change, often undocumented and tied to old technology.
Reverse engineering recovers design information, while reengineering changes structure while preserving required behaviour.
Technical debt is future cost from shortcuts and grows when not repaid.
Impact analysis identifies affected parts before a change, using dependencies, tests and expert review.
Safe change uses small steps, version control, automated tests, review, staged release and rollback.

en.title: Configuration and release management
en.short: Baselines, change control, branching, reproducible builds, artefacts, release planning, versioning, CI/CD and DevOps.

sections.heading: Configuration and baselines
sections.text: Configuration management identifies every configuration item: source files, build scripts, dependencies, database scripts, tests and documents. A baseline is an approved, immutable snapshot of those items at a point in time, labelled so it can be rebuilt and audited. Change control protects baselines: a change request states the reason, impact analysis checks affected items and tests, an authorised person approves or rejects it, and the result is verified and recorded. Version control stores the history, but a baseline adds approval and traceability.

sections.heading: Branching and reproducible builds
sections.text: Branching strategies decide how work diverges. Trunk-based development keeps a shared main line and uses short-lived feature branches; release branches isolate a version being stabilised; long-lived branching models such as GitFlow, which keeps separate develop and main branches, suit scheduled releases but increase merge effort. A build is reproducible when the same source, dependency versions, toolchain and environment produce the same artefact. Pin dependencies with lockfiles, fix compiler and container image versions, and record build metadata. Artefacts are the outputs stored for use: binaries, packages, container images, test reports and documentation, each identified by version.

sections.heading: Release planning and versioning
sections.text: Release planning sets scope, target date, dependencies, risks, acceptance criteria, rollback plan and communication. Semantic versioning labels releases MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. MAJOR changes break compatibility, MINOR adds backward-compatible features, PATCH fixes bugs. Example: release 2.4.1 gains a backward-compatible feature, so it becomes 2.5.0; a bug fix becomes 2.4.2; an incompatible API change becomes 3.0.0. Pre-release and build metadata may be added, but the meaning of the three numbers stays fixed.

sections.heading: CI/CD and DevOps
sections.text: Continuous integration (CI) merges changes frequently and runs automated builds and tests. Continuous delivery keeps every passing build release-ready; continuous deployment sends it to production automatically. A pipeline should build once, test the artefact, store it, and promote the same artefact through environments. DevOps is a culture and set of practices: shared ownership of delivery, automation, small frequent changes, monitoring and fast feedback. It does not remove change control; it makes approved changes smaller and easier to trace.

keyPoints: A baseline is an approved, immutable snapshot of configuration items.
Change control records the request, impact analysis, approval, verification and outcome.
Reproducible builds pin dependencies, toolchain and environment so the same source gives the same artefact.
Semantic versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH to signal compatibility changes.
CI builds and tests every change; CD keeps releases deployable or deploys them automatically.
DevOps combines automation, shared ownership, monitoring and small frequent changes.

en.title: Software project management and estimation
en.short: Work breakdown, Gantt and critical path, team organisation, monitoring, and size and effort estimation.

sections.heading: Breakdown and scheduling
sections.text:
A work breakdown structure (WBS) splits the project into deliverables and work packages small enough to estimate, assign and track. Scheduling orders them, records dependencies and allocates people. A Gantt chart shows each task as a bar against time, making overlap and resource clashes visible.

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks. It sets the shortest possible duration; its tasks have zero float (slack). Example: A=3d, B=4d, C=5d, D=2d; B and C follow A, D follows both. Paths A-B-D=9d and A-C-D=10d, so A-C-D is critical and B has 1d float.

sections.heading: Size and effort estimation
sections.text:
Function points measure functional size from the user’s view. Count external inputs (EI), external outputs (EO), external inquiries (EQ), internal logical files (ILF) and external interface files (EIF), then apply weights. With average weights 4, 5, 4, 10 and 7, unadjusted FP = 4×EI + 5×EO + 4×EQ + 10×ILF + 7×EIF. For 10 EI, 8 EO, 6 EQ, 4 ILF and 2 EIF: 40+40+24+40+14 = 158. Adjust with the 14 general system characteristics: adjusted FP (AFP) = UFP × adjustment factor.

COCOMO estimates effort from size in thousands of lines of code (KLOC): effort = a × KLOC^b × EAF, where a and b depend on project mode and calibration, and EAF is the effort adjustment factor. Story points are relative size units; forecast = backlog points ÷ average velocity. Treat estimates as ranges, because uncertainty is high early and falls as work proceeds.

sections.heading: Teams and monitoring
sections.text: Teams may be organised by function, by project or as a matrix; each has trade-offs in communication and control. Progress monitoring compares planned with actual work using milestones, burn-down charts and earned value. Earned value uses PV (planned value), EV (earned value) and AC (actual cost): cost variance CV = EV − AC, schedule variance SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV. A CPI below 1 means cost overrun; an SPI below 1 means behind schedule.

keyPoints: Critical path is the longest dependent path and has zero float.
Function points: UFP = 4EI + 5EO + 4EQ + 10ILF + 7EIF (average weights).
COCOMO effort = a × KLOC^b × EAF; constants depend on project mode and calibration.
Story-point forecast = backlog points ÷ average velocity.
Earned value: CV = EV − AC and SV = EV − PV; CPI = EV ÷ AC and SPI = EV ÷ PV.
Treat estimates as ranges and re-estimate as uncertainty falls.

en.title: Software quality and process improvement
en.short: Quality models, reviews, audits, measurement, and process improvement with CMMI and ISO 9001.

sections.heading: Quality models
sections.text: Software quality is the degree to which a product satisfies stated and implied needs. ISO/IEC 25010, part of the SQuaRE family, gives an international product quality model. Its characteristics include functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, interaction capability (formerly usability), reliability, security, maintainability, flexibility (formerly portability) and safety. Teams use them as a checklist for requirements and test plans. Pass marks depend on the product and context.

sections.heading: Reviews and audits
sections.text: A review is a structured examination of a work product by a team, usually including people other than the author. A formal technical review, such as an inspection, uses defined roles, entry criteria and a checklist; it finds defects early, when they are cheap to fix. An audit is an independent check that a process or product conforms to agreed standards, plans or regulations. Reviews improve the product; audits judge conformity.

sections.heading: Measurement
sections.text: Measurement turns quality goals into numbers. Define a metric, collect data consistently, and interpret it with care. Goal-Question-Metric (GQM) starts from a goal, asks questions, then chooses metrics. Example: a team wants fewer defects. It measures defect density: defects found ÷ size. If 24 defects are found in 12,000 lines of code, defect density is 24 ÷ 12,000 = 0.002 per line, or 2 per 1,000 lines. A low count may mean weak testing, not high quality.

sections.heading: Process improvement and limits
sections.text: Process improvement changes how work is done to raise quality and productivity. CMMI is a process maturity model originally developed by the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) in the United States. It rates organisations at five maturity levels: initial, managed, defined, quantitatively managed and optimising. ISO 9001 is a generic international standard for a quality management system; an accredited certification body grants certification after an external audit. Both make processes explicit and auditable. But certification is not a product guarantee: it shows conformity at a point in time, can encourage paperwork over engineering, and does not replace testing, reviews or skilled people. Check current editions and appraisal rules with the official bodies.

keyPoints: ISO/IEC 25010 defines product quality characteristics such as reliability, security and maintainability.
Reviews examine work products; audits check conformity against standards or plans.
Defect density = defects found ÷ size, for example 24 ÷ 12,000 = 0.002 per line.
CMMI appraises process maturity at five levels, from initial to optimising.
ISO 9001 certifies a quality management system, not the quality of a product.
Certification is a snapshot and can encourage paperwork; it does not replace testing and skilled people.

en.title: Software security and dependability
en.short: Dependability, risk, safety and reliability, plus secure development, threat modelling and privacy.

sections.heading: Dependability and risk
sections.text:
Dependability is the property that a system’s service can justifiably be trusted. It is an umbrella for reliability, availability, safety, security and maintainability. Security is the ability to protect the system and its data from harm; it is part of dependability, not a separate concern.

Risk management identifies threats, estimates likelihood and impact, chooses controls, and monitors them. A simple risk score is likelihood × impact, using agreed scales. Controls may avoid, reduce, transfer or accept the risk. Record the reasoning, because risks change.

sections.heading: Safety and hazards
sections.text:
A safety-critical system is one whose failure could injure or kill people, damage property or harm the environment. Safety is freedom from unacceptable harm. Hazard analysis finds hazards, their causes and consequences before and during design. Common techniques are HAZOP (guide-word review of deviations), FMEA (failure modes and effects analysis) and fault tree analysis (logic tree from an undesired event to causes). Use more than one view; no technique finds everything.

Reliability is the probability of failure-free operation for a stated time under stated conditions. For a constant failure rate λ, R(t) = e^(−λt). Example: λ = 0.0002 per hour and t = 1,000 hours give R = e^(−0.2) = 0.819, about 82%.

sections.heading: Secure development
sections.text:
Secure development builds security in from requirements to operation. Threat modelling asks what assets need protection, who may attack them, how, and what controls reduce the risk. A data-flow diagram helps. OWASP Top 10 is a widely used awareness list of web application risk categories; the list is revised, so check the current official version.

Input validation checks that data is well formed, in range and authorised before use. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, validate on the server, and encode output for its context. Privacy means limiting personal data to what is needed, protecting it, and respecting consent and legal rules, which differ by country.

keyPoints: Dependability covers reliability, availability, safety, security and maintainability.
Risk management identifies threats, estimates likelihood and impact, applies controls and monitors them.
Hazard analysis techniques include HAZOP, FMEA and fault tree analysis.
Reliability for constant failure rate is R(t) = e^(−λt); λ = 0.0002/h and t = 1,000 h give R ≈ 0.819.
Threat modelling identifies assets, attackers and controls; OWASP Top 10 changes, so check the current version.
Validate input on the server with allow-lists and encode output; protect privacy and follow local law.

en.title: Human-centred design and usability
en.short: User-centred design, personas, prototypes, usability principles, accessibility and usability testing.

sections.heading: Users and design
sections.text:
Human-centred design (HCD) is an iterative approach that puts users’ needs, abilities and context at the centre. ISO 9241-210 describes it for interactive systems. It starts with user research: interviews, observation and task analysis.

A persona is a fictional but research-based representative user, such as a student who shares a phone and has low data. Personas help a team make design decisions for real people, not for itself.

sections.heading: Prototypes and principles
sections.text:
A prototype is an early model of the interface. Low-fidelity prototypes, such as paper sketches, are cheap and expose flow problems early. High-fidelity prototypes behave like the product and test detailed interaction.

Common usability principles include consistency, visible feedback, error prevention, recognition rather than recall, and user control. Usability is the extent to which specified users achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction in a specified context of use (ISO 9241-11).

sections.heading: Accessibility and testing
sections.text:
Accessibility means the product can be used by people with disabilities, including visual, hearing, motor and cognitive impairments. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) organise this as perceivable, operable, understandable and robust.

Usability testing observes representative users attempting realistic tasks, often thinking aloud. Record task success, time on task, errors and satisfaction. Test with people who differ in age, device, language and ability. Fix problems and test again.

sections.heading: Case and quality
sections.text:
Suppose a team at a college in Kano, Nigeria, builds a course registration app. Persona Amina is a second-year student with low vision who uses a low-end Android phone. In a paper prototype test with five students, three register for two courses without help.

One cannot find the submit button because it is below the visible screen area; another finds the form fields unlabelled, so a screen reader could not read them out. The team moves the button, adds labels and retests; all five succeed. Good interface decisions raise task success and reduce rework, support calls and costly late changes, so they improve software quality.

keyPoints: Human-centred design is iterative and based on user research, not assumptions.
Personas are research-based fictional users that guide design decisions.
Prototypes from paper to interactive let teams test ideas before building.
Usability is effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction for specified users and goals.
Accessibility means usable by people with disabilities; WCAG uses POUR principles.
Usability testing measures task success, time, errors and satisfaction with representative users.

en.title: Professional practice and ethics
en.short: Codes, professional bodies, law, IP, data protection and whistleblowing for software engineers.

sections.heading: Codes of ethics
sections.text: The ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice is a joint code from the ACM and the IEEE Computer Society. It has eight principles: public, client and employer, product, judgement, management, profession, colleagues, and self. In plain terms, engineers should put public safety first, deliver good software, keep skills current, respect confidentiality, avoid conflicts of interest, and report serious problems. The code guides conduct but does not replace the law of your country.

sections.heading: Professional bodies
sections.text: Professional bodies set standards and support engineers. Examples are the ACM, the IEEE Computer Society, the BCS (British Computer Society), and, in Nigeria, the Computer Professionals Registration Council of Nigeria (CPN). They publish codes, run continuing professional development, and may register or certify members. Registration and licensing rules vary by country: some titles are protected by law, others are voluntary. Check the current rules of the body and the law where you work.

sections.heading: Law and intellectual property
sections.text: Software work is shaped by contract, employment, liability and intellectual property (IP) law.
