IP includes copyright, which protects the expression of code but not the idea; patents, which may cover inventions and vary by jurisdiction; trade secrets, which protect confidential algorithms; and trademarks, which protect names and logos. Licences matter. Case: Ngozi in Lagos builds a payroll app. She uses an MIT-licensed library, which allows reuse with attribution, and a proprietary database, which needs a paid licence. She checks both licences and the client contract before release.

sections.heading: Data protection and whistleblowing
sections.text: Data protection law controls personal data. It requires a lawful basis, data minimisation, security, and breach reporting. Examples are the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, the EU GDPR, and the UK Data Protection Act 2018. Whistleblowing is reporting wrongdoing. Protections vary: some countries shield whistleblowers from retaliation, others do not. Case: Tunde finds a health app sending patient names to an unsecured server. He reports it to his manager, keeps records, and if nothing is done, contacts the data protection authority. He checks local law and company policy.

keyPoints: The ACM/IEEE-CS code has eight principles, from public interest to self-improvement.
Professional bodies such as ACM, IEEE Computer Society, BCS and CPN set standards and may register members.
Copyright protects code expression, while patents, trade secrets and trademarks protect other kinds of work.
Data protection law requires lawful use, minimisation, security and breach reporting for personal data.
Whistleblowing protections vary by country, so check local law and company policy before reporting.
Always check the current law and registration rules of the country where you work.

en.title: Software engineering capstone project
en.short: Running a team capstone from requirements and plan through design, build, testing, demo and reflection.

sections.heading: The capstone brief
sections.text:
A capstone project is a team project that runs over a term or a year and asks you to build a software system from start to finish. It integrates separate courses: you apply requirements, design, testing and management methods together under one deadline.

A supervisor or client sets the brief. Team size varies by institution; three to six students is common. The deliverable is a working, documented system plus evidence of how the team worked, not code alone.

sections.heading: Plan and control
sections.text:
Agree a scope statement: what the system will and will not do. Turn it into a baseline requirements list and dated milestones, for example requirements frozen by week 4, design by week 6, first build by week 9, delivery by week 12.

Keep a risk register, a table of each risk, its likelihood, impact and mitigating action. Adaeze’s team, building a clinic booking system in Ibadan, might rate server failure as medium likelihood and high impact, and keep a local backup for the demo. Hold weekly meetings and keep minutes and a decision log.

sections.heading: Build, test, show
sections.text:
Design before coding, but keep design notes short and current. Use a shared repository and a simple branching rule.

Test at unit, integration and acceptance level. A traceability table links each requirement to at least one test, which gives evidence of coverage.

Documentation normally includes requirements, design notes, test plan and results, a user guide and a final report. The demonstration walks through the main use cases live or recorded; rehearse it and prepare a fallback if the network fails. Delivery includes a handover of the repository, build instructions and user guide.

sections.heading: Reflect on process
sections.text:
The reflection is a short written account of what the team planned, what happened and what you would change. Cover process and teamwork: roles, communication, estimation and testing.

Support it with meeting minutes, commit history and test logs. Each member states their contribution. Honest analysis is more valuable than claiming everything went perfectly.

keyPoints: A capstone integrates requirements, design, construction, testing and delivery in one team project.
Agree a scope baseline and dated milestones before building.
Keep a risk register with likelihood, impact and mitigation for each risk.
Link requirements to tests with a traceability table and keep documentation current.
Demonstrate the working system and hand over repository, build instructions and user guide.
Reflect honestly on process and teamwork using minutes, commits and test logs as evidence.

en.title: Advanced software architecture
en.short: Architecture-centric development, quality scenarios, tactics, ATAM, and service and product-line trade-offs.

sections.heading: Architecture as centre
sections.text: Architecture-centric development treats architecture as the primary design artifact and the basis for planning, team structure and evaluation. Quality attributes such as performance, security and modifiability are expressed as quality attribute scenarios: source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response, response measure. Example: "A payment service, under normal load, must reject a duplicate request within 200 ms." This turns vague goals like "fast" or "reliable" into testable requirements. Tactics are design decisions that achieve such responses, e.g. heartbeat for availability, caching for performance, encapsulation for modifiability.

sections.heading: Evaluation and ATAM
sections.text: Architecture evaluation checks architecture against scenarios before costly build. ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method, from SEI) gathers stakeholders, presents business drivers and the architecture, builds a utility tree ranking scenarios by importance and difficulty, analyses the architecture against them, and records risks, non-risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points. A sensitivity point affects one quality attribute; a tradeoff point affects two or more in opposite directions. ATAM does not score architecture; it exposes decisions for negotiation. CBAM extends it with cost/benefit.

sections.heading: Service approaches
sections.text: Microservices split a system into small independently deployable services around business capabilities, often with separate data stores. They favour team autonomy and selective scaling but add network failure, data consistency and operations burden. Service-oriented architecture (SOA) exposes reusable enterprise services, often through an enterprise service bus and strong governance. It favours integration and reuse but can centralise control and slow change. Both need clear service contracts and ownership.

sections.heading: Product lines and organisation
sections.text: A software product line manages a family of products from shared core assets and explicit variability. Domain engineering builds the platform; application engineering derives products. It rewards long-term reuse and faster variants but needs upfront investment, roadmaps and coordination. Architecture also follows organisation: Conway’s law says system structures mirror communication structures. Choose microservices for autonomous teams, SOA for enterprise integration, product lines for planned families, and evaluate the organisational cost.

keyPoints: Architecture-centric development makes architecture the main artifact for meeting quality attributes and organising teams.
A quality attribute scenario has source, stimulus, environment, artifact, response and response measure.
Architecture tactics are design decisions that achieve quality attributes; ATAM exposes risks, sensitivity points and tradeoff points.
Microservices give independent deployment and team autonomy but add distributed-system and operational costs.
SOA emphasises reusable enterprise services and governance, often through an enterprise service bus.
Software product lines gain long-term reuse from shared assets and variability but need upfront investment and coordination.

en.title: Formal specification and verification
en.short: This summary covers Z, B and Alloy specifications, model checking, theorem proving, refinement and their limits.

sections.heading: Specifications in Z, B and Alloy
sections.text:
Formal specification writes requirements in a language with precise syntax and semantics, so ambiguity is removed. Z is an ISO standard (ISO/IEC 13568:2002).

Z uses sets, relations and schemas: a schema groups variable declarations and a predicate; state schemas carry the invariant and operation schemas give preconditions and postconditions. B and Event-B use abstract machines and refinement. Alloy uses relational logic and a small declarative syntax; its Analyzer searches for small counterexamples within a bounded scope.

sections.heading: Checking and proving
sections.text:
Verification asks whether a model satisfies a property. Model checking explores all reachable states of a finite model and returns a counterexample when a property fails. It is automatic but suffers state explosion, where the states to explore grow too fast to store.

Theorem proving derives properties from axioms and definitions. It can handle infinite state and inductive proofs, but usually needs expert guidance and may be interactive.

sections.heading: Refinement and invariants
sections.text:
Refinement links an abstract specification to a more concrete design or implementation. Each concrete operation must preserve the abstract behaviour and not introduce new observable outcomes.

An invariant is a property true in every reachable state, such as borrowed(b) ≤ copies(b) for each book b. A library case: Ada borrows one of two copies of a book; the invariant stops a third loan. The concrete model must keep the count.

sections.heading: Tools, cost and limits
sections.text:
Tool support includes Z/Eves and ProofPower for Z, Rodin for Event-B, the Alloy Analyzer, and model checkers such as SPIN and NuSMV; Coq, Isabelle/HOL and PVS support theorem proving.

Formal methods cost training, specification effort and proof maintenance. They suit critical or subtle designs, not every project. A proof only concerns the model, so wrong assumptions or a poor model still mislead.

keyPoints: Formal specification removes ambiguity by writing requirements in a language with precise syntax and semantics.
Z uses schemas, B and Event-B use abstract machines and refinement, and Alloy uses relational logic with bounded analysis.
Model checking explores finite reachable states automatically and returns counterexamples, but state explosion limits it.
Theorem proving can handle infinite state and inductive proofs, but needs expertise and may be interactive.
Refinement must preserve abstract behaviour, and invariants must hold in every reachable state.
Formal methods cost training and proof maintenance, and a proof is only as good as the model and its assumptions.

en.title: Empirical software engineering research
en.short: Experiments, case studies, surveys, reviews and repository mining, with validity, replication and ethics.

sections.heading: Study designs
sections.text: An experiment manipulates one or more independent variables, such as a review technique, and measures dependent variables, such as defect detection, under controlled conditions. Random assignment and control groups support causal claims. A case study examines a phenomenon in its real context, often one project or team, and is strong for explanation but weak for generalisation. A survey collects self-reported data from a sample; good sampling and validated questions matter. Example: a case study of 12 pull requests finds 9 merged, 75%, but n=12 gives wide uncertainty.

sections.heading: Reviews and mining
sections.text: A systematic literature review follows a written protocol: research questions, search strings, databases, inclusion and exclusion criteria, quality assessment and synthesis. It reduces bias but is slow. Repository mining extracts data from version control, issue trackers and app stores. It can study many projects, but data are observational and often noisy. Example: mining 1,000 commits can show change patterns, not prove causes.

sections.heading: Measurement and validity
sections.text: Measurement turns constructs, meaning abstract concepts such as code quality, into variables. Define each metric and check reliability. Threats to validity: construct validity (does the metric measure the concept?), internal validity (could another factor explain the result?), external validity (do findings generalise?) and conclusion validity (are statistical inferences sound?). Report threats honestly and use triangulation, meaning more than one method or data source.

sections.heading: Replication and ethics
sections.text: Replication tests whether findings hold with new data or settings. Exact replication repeats the design; conceptual replication changes materials or population. For a dissertation, obtain ethics approval where required, seek informed consent, protect personal data, anonymise participants and repositories, and report methods and limitations so others can judge and repeat the work. Keep data secure and follow your institution’s rules.

keyPoints: Experiments manipulate variables under control; case studies study real contexts; surveys collect self-reports.
Systematic reviews use a protocol; repository mining analyses existing project data.
Define metrics and assess construct, internal, external and conclusion validity.
Replication can be exact or conceptual and strengthens confidence.
Ethics approval where required, informed consent for human participants, and privacy and anonymisation for personal and repository data.
Report methods, data and limitations so others can judge and repeat the work.
